name: liquid N2 at 77 K
paper: H. Augustin, "Über die Dichte des flüssigen Wasserstoffs, den Brechungsexponenten und die Dispersion des flüssigen Wasserstoffs und des flüssigen Stickstoffs", Ann. Phys. 351 (1915) 419–445, DOI 10.1002/andp.19153510307
source: n(λ) = 1.19573 + 0.00106457 µm² ÷ λ², a two-term Cauchy fit made here to Augustin's absolute indices of chemically prepared, argon-free liquid N2 at −195.83 °C (77.32 K), 1.19841, 1.19873, 1.19917, 1.20141 (±5 × 10⁻⁵) at 656.3, 579.0, 546.1, 435.9 nm (p. 443, the wavelengths p. 438's), read from the article's scan, Zenodo record 1514490 (CC0), https://zenodo.org/api/records/1514490/files/article.pdf/content, SHA-256 b7c6905a0ae90c3c2bd668cc4c5d738271a24e06e1e1e278a6cdfb4ff29e4bf3, fetched 2026-10-14. The fit's residuals are -2.1e-4, 1.8e-4, 1.3e-4, -7.7e-5: the 656.3 nm value lies above the line that the other three and N2's gas dispersion give. The other measurements agree: Johns and Wilhelm 1937 (Can. J. Res. 15a, 101, DOI 10.1139/cjr37a-013; closed), whose abstract gives 1.1990 at 546.1 nm at the normal boiling point; Liveing and Dewar 1893's 1.2053 at the D line (Phil. Mag. (5) 36, 328) was of nitrogen with about 5% O2. k = 0: no measurement of liquid N2's visible absorption was found, and Liveing and Dewar call it colourless. The Lorentz–Lorenz method's checks on measured liquids (gas dispersions as view/atmosphere/rayleigh.ts holds them, at each liquid's molar density from the NIST Chemistry WebBook): liquid Ar at 90 K against Sinnock and Smith 1969 (Phys. Rev. 181, 1297), +0.0023 at 546.1 nm; liquid N2 at 77.32 K against Augustin 1915 (Ann. Phys. 351, 419), +0.0019 at 546.1 nm; liquid CH4 at 90.694 K against Martonchik and Orton 1994's 90 K (Appl. Opt. 33, 8306), +0.0074 at 583.1 nm; liquid NH3 at 239.80 K against Wong and Anderson 1972 (J. Opt. Soc. Am. 62, 219), +0.0057 at 632.8 nm
licence: measured values cited as facts, from a public-domain article (Zenodo's copy, CC0), and a fit made here; no data set is copied
reduction: the fit evaluated on 380–780 nm every 5 nm, to six significant figures, beyond the data's 435.9–656.3 nm by extrapolation; k = 0. Augustin's wavelengths are the lines' in air, read as vacuum wavelengths (under 5 × 10⁻⁶ in n); 77 K stands for his 77.32 K, a little below the normal boiling point, 77.355 K
